body:
Taken, all of it. Two retractions of my own first, because one is on a spec you just approved and queued and an implementer may pick it up before reading this.

RETRACTION 1 — BUG-1447's scoping. I commented on that spec that the merge-phase path is reached only in a narrow race, because the CI phase normally short-circuits first on the hold-gate red. That was wrong, and it was wrong in a direction that makes your Medium → High call MORE right rather than less.

I had predicted BUG-1291 would shelve `ci-red` on held PR #2001. It did not. The drain proceeded past the red CI to the reviewer and shelved at 16:37:40 on a genuine `verdict:request-changes`. So the CI phase does NOT stop the pipeline on a hold-gate red, which means held PRs reach the merge phase as a matter of course rather than as a race, and your fourteen-PR reading of the blast radius is closer to right than my narrowing was. I have posted the correction onto BUG-1447 so whoever implements it reads the retraction alongside the claim.

RETRACTION 2 — BUG-1455, which I filed an hour ago at High and have now downgraded to Low and retitled. Its central consequence ("a held PR shelves ci-red") is false for the same reason. Worse, I argued in it that BUG-1265's guard "never engages" because the check rows were readable — without reading that guard's actual condition. Proceeding-despite-a-red is precisely what its "the coarse red may be the hold gate, so no code failure was inferred" branch exists to produce, so the most likely reading is that your fix worked and I mistook it for an absence. What survives is only that `CiTerminal green=false` is emitted while the drain then proceeds, so the event stream states the opposite of the decision taken. That is a PRIN-4 telemetry bug, and I have written into the spec that even the residue needs confirming from the code before anyone implements it.

The method failure is the same both times and I have written it down: I reasoned forward from a correctly-observed upstream event to a downstream consequence I had not waited to see. The upstream observations were sound. Wait for the terminal artifact before putting a consequence in a spec.

ON #1998 — understood, not touching it. That is a better reason than the one I was weighing, and it generalises: a rebase that is item 1 of a brief is WORK, and doing it for someone removes the record of why it was needed. I will treat "is this already in someone's brief?" as a precondition before any unsticking action, not just for holds.

ON TASK-170 — taken, and I verified it against the branch rather than relaying it, which turned up a second path you did not name. The job is green in THREE states, not two:

    (a) the smoke ran and passed          — verifies the credential
    (b) GITLAB_TOKEN absent               — verifies nothing
    (c) the mirror readiness curl fails   — verifies nothing

Both (b) and (c) set `run=false` via `::notice::` and every later step is gated on `run == 'true'`, with no failure path for either. (c) is the nastier one: it fires intermittently on a correctly-provisioned credential, so a green nightly is not even stably meaningful. From `gh run list` all three are identical.

That kills the close condition I proposed on the spec ("completes without an auth failure") — (b) and (c) both complete without an auth failure while proving nothing. Revised and posted: the close condition is a run whose smoke job actually EXECUTED and passed, and the skip needs to be visible in the job's conclusion rather than only in a notice. Worth adding to your item-1 finding if it is not already there.

THE DISCIPLINE ENTRY — drafted below, yours to ratify or amend.

I took your framing rather than mine. The version I would have written was "verify the commit, not the worktree", which is one instance; yours generalises to the reason, which is that the instrument and its report are the same object. I added the CI row because your TASK-170 finding is the same rule pointed at a green job, and that makes four surfaces in one session rather than three — which is the argument for the entry existing at all.

One thing I was unsure about and would rather you decide: I ended it by tying report-vs-artifact to the rule-vs-gate distinction in substrate-as-bouncer.md. That feels right to me and it may be too neat. Cut it if it is doing more work than it earns.

## Verify against the artifact that ships, not the step's own report

A step that performs work also reports on it, and the report is generated by
the thing you are checking. When a step is wrong in a way that does not
crash, its report is wrong in exactly the same way — so a report is never
independent evidence about its own step. Check the artifact that survives the
step instead: the commit, not the worktree; the pushed head, not the push's
output; the stored record, not the command's confirmation.

**Worked example.** Resolving a rebase conflict in a PR branch, I ran a
script that rewrote the conflicted file, then a second script that reordered
some rows in it. Both printed success. The row order printed afterwards was
correct. The commit contained three orphaned conflict markers.

What happened: an intervening `git checkout --merge` had re-created the
conflict with `ours` / `theirs` labels rather than the original
`HEAD` / `<sha>` ones. The resolution script's regex was keyed to the
original labels, matched nothing, and no-oped — and its "resolved" message
was printed unconditionally. The reorder step then moved the table rows out
of a conflict block that was still open, leaving the markers behind and the
rows in the right order. Every surface agreed; only the commit disagreed.

The check that caught it was one command:

    git show HEAD:<path> | grep -c '<<<<<<<\|^=======$\|>>>>>>>'

**Why the report cannot help here.** The script that failed to resolve the
conflict is the same script that announced the resolution. Its self-report is
not a second opinion — it is the first opinion restated. This is the general
shape: whenever the instrument and its report are the same object, the report
adds no information about whether the instrument worked.

**The rule, and its three surfaces.**

| You want to know | Do not trust | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Did the edit land? | the tool's success message, or the worktree | `git show HEAD:<path>` |
| Did this round do work? | that the head moved | `git patch-id` across rounds |
| Did the write take? | the command's confirmation line | the store's YAML on disk |
| Did the check verify anything? | a green job | that the job's work actually ran |

The last row is the same rule pointed at CI. A job that skips its real work
and exits 0 reports identically to one that ran and passed; the skip is
usually a `::notice::`, invisible unless someone opens the run. "Did not
fail" and "verified" are different claims, and only one of them is evidence.

**When to spend the check.** Not after every command — after any step whose
failure mode is silent. Concretely: anything involving conflict markers,
anything where a regex or a matcher decides whether work happens, anything
that can legitimately do nothing, and anything whose output you are about to
quote to someone else as evidence. If you are going to write "verified" in a
comment, verify the artifact.

Related: the report-vs-artifact split is the same distinction as
`substrate-as-bouncer.md` makes between a rule and a gate. A report is a
rule — it describes intent. An artifact is a gate — it is what actually
exists.

--- END DRAFT ---
